steps.title: Put on goggles
steps.instruction: Electrolysis makes chlorine, a toxic gas, and sodium hydroxide, which is corrosive. Goggles on, room ventilated, low voltage only.

whatIf.no_ppe: A single splash in an unprotected eye can cause lasting damage, which is why goggles go on before any bottle is opened.

steps.title: 50 mL brine into the cell
steps.instruction: Pour about 50 mL of brine into the cell so both carbon electrodes are covered.

steps.title: A few drops of universal indicator
steps.instruction: Add 3 to 5 drops of universal indicator. It starts green: neutral.

steps.title: Tube over the cathode
steps.instruction: Hold the collection tube upside down over the negative electrode (cathode) to catch its gas.

steps.title: Switch on
steps.instruction: Switch the power pack on (6 V d.c.).

whatIf.wrong_amount: A higher voltage makes chlorine much faster, which quickly becomes dangerous in a closed room.

steps.title: Collect the hydrogen
steps.instruction: Watch bubbles at both electrodes and wait until a little gas has collected.

steps.title: Test the anode gas
steps.instruction: Hold damp blue litmus paper near the positive electrode (anode). Do not sniff the gas.

whatIf.no_ppe: Chlorine attacks the lining of the nose, throat and lungs even in small amounts.

steps.title: Switch off
steps.instruction: Switch the power pack off before testing the hydrogen.

steps.title: Light the Bunsen
steps.instruction: Light the Bunsen burner so you can light a splint.

steps.title: Light a splint
steps.instruction: Hold the splint in the flame until it catches.

steps.title: The pop test
steps.instruction: Bring the lit splint to the mouth of the collection tube.

safe-2.text: Pick up the goggles and put them on before you touch any bottle.

brine-1.text: The electrodes need to be in the solution.

brine-2.text: Pick up the brine bottle and pour about 50 mL into the cell.

ind-1.text: An indicator will show any change in pH.

ind-2.text: Add a few drops of universal indicator to the cell.

collect-1.text: The gas from the negative electrode is worth collecting.

collect-2.text: Pick up the empty tube and choose Hold over, then the cell.

collect-3.text: Watch the tube go over the cathode.

power-2.text: Select the cell and choose the power button.

gas-2.text: Wait (or speed up time) until about 2 mL of gas has collected.

litmus-2.text: Pick up the litmus paper and choose Hold near, then the cell.

burn-1.text: You need a flame to light the splint.

burn-2.text: Light the Bunsen, then hold the splint in the flame.

burn-3.text: Watch the burner light and the splint catch.

pop-1.text: Which gas burns with a squeaky pop?

pop-2.text: Bring the lit splint to the collection tube's mouth.

observations.whatHappened: Bubbles streamed off both electrodes. The gas from the cathode burned with a squeaky pop. The gas at the anode turned damp litmus red and then bleached it white, and smelled of swimming pools. The indicator turned from green to purple.
observations.why: Brine contains Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. At the negative cathode, hydrogen ions (from water) gain electrons more easily than sodium ions, so hydrogen gas forms. At the positive anode, chloride ions lose electrons to form chlorine gas, which bleaches damp litmus. Sodium and hydroxide ions are left behind, so the solution becomes sodium hydroxide: alkaline, and the indicator turns purple.
realWorld: The chlor-alkali industry makes chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide
Chlorine for clean drinking water and bleach
Sodium hydroxide for soap and paper

prompts.question: Which gas forms at the negative electrode (cathode)?
prompts.explain: H⁺ ions gain electrons: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. It burns with a squeaky pop.

prompts.question: How do you know the anode gas is chlorine?
prompts.explain: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus (often turning it red first).

prompts.question: Why did the indicator turn purple?
choices: Sodium hydroxide is left in the solution, making it alkaline
prompts.explain: Removing H⁺ and Cl⁻ leaves Na⁺ and OH⁻: sodium hydroxide solution.

captions.text: Goggles on. Brine is sodium chloride dissolved in water.
Universal indicator: green, so the brine starts neutral.
Power on. Ions move: positive ions to the cathode (−), negative ions to the anode (+).
Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode. Purple indicator: sodium hydroxide is being left behind.
Damp litmus near the anode: red, then bleached. That's chlorine.
Squeaky pop: the cathode gas is hydrogen.
